title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what a figure does not say

questions.prompt: A ministry announces that primary school enrolment in a district has climbed from 61 % to 88 % in three years. A journalist writes that 88 % of the district's children of primary age are now sitting in a classroom every day. Why is his sentence claiming more than the figure allows?

options.text: the figure counts only the children who passed their end-of-year examination in the third year
the figure counts names put down on a register, and a name on a list can belong to an empty chair
a share of a population cannot be turned into a number of children without the size of the district
the 88 per cent is an average taken across the three years, so no single year ever reached it

questions.explanation: Registration and presence are two different counts, taken at two different moments and by two different means. One is done once, in September, with a pen and a list; the other is done every morning, by looking at the room. The ministry has published the first and the journalist has reported the second, and nothing in the announcement bridges the gap: a child registered in September may have stopped coming by March without a single figure moving. The objection about arithmetic is a true statement that leaves the trouble untouched, since what the journalist claimed was a proportion and not a head count. The objection about the three years misreads the announcement outright: the climb took three years, but 88 per cent is where the climb arrived, the figure the district stands at now, and not an average spread over the three. And no examination has been mentioned anywhere.

questions.prompt: A village has three hundred children of primary age whom no school has ever taken in, and the handful of others who do reach the classroom arrive at midday with nothing to eat. Tick EVERY body on this list whose stated business covers part of that problem.

options.text: UNICEF
UNESCO
the WFP
OPEC
the IMF
the WTO

questions.explanation: The village has two troubles and three doors. Children's rights, and the food, health care and schooling that go with them, are what the children's fund of the United Nations was set up for in 1946; getting three hundred children into a classroom is a matter of education, and education, science and culture are what the body founded in 1945 was created to work on; and the fight against hunger, run from Rome since 1963, is what the food programme does, which is exactly the midday half of the problem. The remaining three name their own field as soon as you unfold their letters, and not one of those fields is either of the village's troubles: a club of oil producers, a fund for the money of nations, and a body that deals in the trade between them. That is what expanding an acronym settles - not how large or how useful a body is, only what it is about, and oil, currency and customs bring nothing to a register with three hundred names missing from it or to a classroom that has not eaten.

questions.prompt: A pie chart is headed "Regional distribution of children out of school, 2001/02". The slice given to the industrialized countries reads 2.3 %. Two point three per cent of what?

options.text: of all the children living in the industrialized countries
of all the schools standing in the industrialized countries
of all the children of primary age alive in the world
of all the children in the world who were out of school

questions.explanation: The word that decides is the one in the heading: a distribution answers where, never how badly. So the circle is cut out of a single quantity - the children the whole world had left outside a classroom that year, all 115 million of them - and each slice says what portion of them lived in one region. Read it as a rate instead and you are dividing by a completely different number, the children those countries hold altogether, which this chart nowhere prints; that reading needs a second figure it cannot give you. Buildings are not on the chart at all, and the world's whole population of primary age is a far larger quantity than the one being shared out here.

questions.prompt: A pupil has learnt that unless hides a not inside it. Asked to rewrite "Unless the road is cleared, the bus will turn back at the bridge" with if, he writes: "If the road is not cleared, the bus will not turn back at the bridge." Where, if anywhere, has he gone wrong, and why?

options.text: the first half, because the verb behind if had to stay positive, unless meaning the same as if
neither half, because a sentence rewritten out of unless comes out with two negatives in it
the second half, because unless governs only the clause it opens and leaves the other verb alone
the second half, because a sentence that opens on if is not allowed a second negative further along

questions.explanation: He was right about the word and wrong about its reach. Turning unless into if not is exactly the trade the rule describes, and his opening clause performs it correctly - so the sentence cannot be left as it stands: there is one negative in play here, the one that was hiding inside the word, and he has spent it twice. The bus was turning back in the sentence he started from, and it must still be turning back in the one he finishes with, since nothing in the original ever made that half negative. Nor is there any rule against a second negative further along: if you do not help us, we shall not finish carries one in each clause and is an ordinary sentence. What rules one out here is simply that the sentence he was handed had none in that half. And the reading that makes the two words interchangeable gets the whole meaning backwards.

questions.prompt: In an advertisement, only the first few letters of some words are printed and the missing letters are shown as dots, one dot for one letter. A line reads "Give to us today and you give a child a ch...." Four six-letter words open on those two letters. Which one does the sentence want?

options.text: chance
choice
change
charge

questions.explanation: The shape has settled nothing: all four open on the same two letters and all four run to six. So the sentence has to do the deciding, and what a charity holds out to a child is an opportunity he did not have before - a way into a classroom, a year he would otherwise have lost. Offering him a choice would mean putting two roads in front of a child who at present has none; offering him a change would promise only that something will be different, without saying it will be better; and a charge is money asked of somebody, which is the last thing a page begging for gifts would say it was handing out.

questions.prompt: A sentence handed down under Aristotle's name compares knowledge to a fountain, and warns that the fountain dries up unless new streams keep running into it. Turned into plain words about a person, what is it claiming?

options.text: a mind that takes in too much at once will keep none of it for long
a mind is filled once in youth and lives on that store ever after
a mind that has been filled deeply enough needs nothing added to it later
a mind that takes in nothing new does not hold what it has; it empties

questions.explanation: Everything turns on the word the saying is built round. A fountain does not need to be emptied to run dry; it runs dry the moment nothing is being poured in, and that is why the sentence is a condition and not a description. Carried over to a person, it makes learning the price of keeping what has already been learnt, so stopping is itself a kind of losing. The picture of a mind swamped by too much at once is a different complaint altogether, and the two comfortable readings - a store laid down in youth, or a point past which one may stop - are precisely what a fountain that dries up is there to deny.
